tagline: From Ohio River boatbuilding to coal country and Nelsonville’s star-patterned paving bricks.
intro: The Appalachian Byway follows SR 78 from Clarington on the Ohio River to Nelsonville, crossing the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains. Ohio’s byway program promotes the foothill landscape along this 105-mile drive; SR 78 is an Ohio Scenic Byway within the Appalachian Byway. Its stretch along the south side of Burr Oak State Park has extreme curves and views, with the local nickname “Rim of the World” sometimes applied to it.

Much of SR 78 passes through former coal-producing areas. The scale of that work survives in Big Muskie’s bucket: the dragline mined coal from 1969 to 1991, then was dismantled in 1999. Its bucket became a centerpiece at Miners’ Memorial Park, while 10,000 acres it had stripped and that were later reclaimed became the wildlife park The Wilds. Nelsonville’s industrial story also involved clay: local manufacturers made glazed paving bricks, some carrying a star pattern that survives in the town’s sidewalks.

Begin at Clarington, where packet boats were built near the mouth of Sunfish Creek. Travel west to the mining memorial, then McConnelsville, where SR 78 crosses the Muskingum to Malta. Beyond the Burr Oak curves, the road passes through Glouster and reaches Nelsonville, where locally made paving bricks remain in the public square’s sidewalks.

moments.title: Clarington
moments.text: Packet boats took shape near the mouth of Sunfish Creek, where Mozena Brothers Boat Yard built steam vessels for western rivers. Clarington grew into a busy river port in the mid-1800s, employing residents in its boat yard alongside businesses serving the town. The yard built Liberty in 1912; artist Ruston Baker’s mural of the boat can be seen in town. Boatbuilding declined in the late 1920s and Mozena Brothers sold the yard, but barges, small ferries and other craft continued to be built here until 1941. The Ohio Valley River Museum preserves the town’s steamboat and river-industry history.

moments.title: Miners' Memorial Park
moments.text: Big Muskie’s bucket could hold two Greyhound buses side by side. The machine that carried it stood 22 stories tall and mined Ohio coal from 1969 to 1991. When the dragline was dismantled for scrap in 1999, the bucket survived and was moved to a park later renamed to honor southeastern Ohio’s coal miners. An information center tells the history of the Central Ohio Coal Company. The memorial pairs that immense piece of equipment with the people who worked in the industry: a memorial honors miners killed on the job, and a Wall of Honor lists Central Ohio Coal Company employees.

moments.title: Morgan County Dungeon
moments.text: The Morgan County Dungeon came back to light during excavation in 1964. This small stone jail held people convicted of offenses including larceny, rioting and adultery. Later relocated to Main Street and preserved, it is marked by an Ohio Historical Marker.

moments.title: Nelsonville
moments.text: Some of Nelsonville’s paving bricks carry a star pattern, and many remain in sidewalks on the public square and in the historic district. Local companies used the area’s dense clay to make them. The Nelsonville Brick Company began its extensive operations in 1877, adding kilns and stacks in 1880 as it expanded. The company’s Nelsonville Block had a salt-glazed surface that made it watertight and gave it a distinctive finish. The Great Depression and the use of concrete contributed to its closure in 1937. The main plant is gone, but some kilns and stacks from the 1880 expansion remain at Brick Kiln Park.
moments.notice: Look for star-patterned paving bricks in the public square’s sidewalks.
